subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 13. In this unit you will study probability – the branch of mathematics that measures how likely things are to happen. Every day you meet uncertainty. Will it rain before sunset? Will the bus from Eastleigh arrive on time? If Amina draws a bead from a bag without looking, what colour is she most likely to pull out? Probability gives you a precise, mathematical way to answer questions like these instead of just guessing.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Understand how to find the theoretical probabilities of equally likely combined events.
Understand that complementary events are two events that have a total probability of 1.
Design and conduct chance experiments or simulations, using small and large numbers of trials. Compare the experimental probabilities with theoretical outcomes.
Understand that tables, diagrams and lists can be used to identify all mutually exclusive outcomes of combined events (independent events only).

outcomes: Describe probability as a measure of likelihood on a scale from 0 to 1.
Calculate theoretical probability for equally likely outcomes using the basic formula.
Express a probability as a fraction, decimal or percentage and convert between them.
Find the probability of an event not happening using the complement.
Add probabilities for mutually exclusive events.
Run experiments to find experimental probability (relative frequency) and compare it with theory.
Use the idea of expected frequency to predict results over many trials.
List all outcomes with a sample space diagram or two-way table.

concepts.title: The Probability Scale
concepts.explanation:
Probability measures how likely an event is, using a number between 0 and 1. Think of it as a ruler. At the far left, 0 means the event is impossible – it can never happen. At the far right, 1 means the event is certain – it must happen. Exactly halfway, at 0.5, the event has an even chance: it is just as likely to happen as not.

It helps to picture the scale like a road with markers along it: 0, then 0.25, then 0.5, then 0.75, then 1. Near 0 the event is very unlikely; near 1 it is very likely; around the middle it could easily go either way. Rolling a 7 on an ordinary die sits at 0; the sun rising tomorrow sits at 1; a fair coin landing on heads sits at exactly 0.5.

Because every probability lies between 0 and 1, you have a built-in check on your own work. If you ever calculate a probability that is negative, or greater than 1, you have made a mistake somewhere – stop and find it. A probability of 2, or of −0.3, simply cannot exist. This single rule, 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, will catch many errors before they cost you marks.
concepts.example: We can write probability in three equivalent ways: as a fraction such as 1/4, as a decimal such as 0.25, or as a percentage such as 25%. They all mean the same thing. To turn a fraction into a decimal, divide the top by the bottom; to turn a decimal into a percentage, multiply by 100. So 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%. Being comfortable moving between these three forms is a skill you will use throughout the unit, so practise it until it feels automatic.

concepts.title: Theoretical Probability
concepts.explanation:
When all outcomes are equally likely – as with a fair coin, a fair die, or a well-shuffled deck – we can work out probability by pure reasoning, without doing any experiment at all. This is called theoretical probability, and it comes from one formula:

P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of possible outcomes.

A favourable outcome simply means an outcome that counts as the event you want – there is nothing lucky or unlucky about the word. Suppose you roll a fair six-sided die. The total number of possible outcomes is 6, because the die can show 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6. The probability of rolling a 3 is 1/6, because just one of those six outcomes is a 3. The probability of rolling an even number is 3/6 = 1/2, because three outcomes (2, 4 and 6) are even.

Consider a spinner divided into 8 equal sections: 3 are red, 2 blue, 2 green and 1 yellow. Because the sections are equal, each is equally likely, so the total is 8. Then P(red) = 3/8 = 0.375, P(blue) = 2/8 = 1/4 = 0.25, P(green) = 2/8 = 1/4, and P(yellow) = 1/8 = 0.125. Notice something important: if you add all four probabilities you get 3/8 + 2/8 + 2/8 + 1/8 = 8/8 = 1. The probabilities of all the separate outcomes always add up to 1, because one of them is certain to happen.
concepts.example: This 'sum to 1' rule is another powerful check. If Yusuf calculates the chances of the four spinner colours and they add up to more than 1, he knows at once that he has slipped somewhere. Keep it in your toolkit alongside the 0-to-1 rule from Concept 1.

concepts.title: Complementary and Mutually Exclusive Events
concepts.explanation:
The complement of an event A is simply 'A does not happen'. Because an event either happens or it does not, these two possibilities must together cover everything, so their probabilities add to 1. That gives a very useful rule:

P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

Using the spinner from Concept 2, P(red) = 3/8, so P(not red) = 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 = 0.625. This shortcut saves a lot of work. To find the chance of 'not red' the long way you would add P(blue) + P(green) + P(yellow); the complement lets you subtract from 1 in a single step. Whenever a question asks for 'at least one' or 'not', think about whether the complement is quicker.

Two events are mutually exclusive when they cannot both happen at the same time. On a single die roll, 'rolling a 2' and 'rolling a 5' are mutually exclusive, because one roll cannot be both a 2 and a 5. When events are mutually exclusive, you find the chance of one or the other by adding:

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) (only when A and B are mutually exclusive).

So the probability of rolling a 2 or a 5 is 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. Be careful: this addition only works when the events cannot overlap. If two events can happen together – for example 'rolling an even number' and 'rolling a number greater than 3' both include the outcome 6 – then simply adding would count the shared outcome twice. In that general case you subtract the overlap: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). For now, most of our 'or' problems will use mutually exclusive events, where plain addition is correct.
concepts.example: A quick way to picture mutually exclusive events is two baskets that never share an item: an outcome drops into one basket or the other, never both. When the baskets can share – the same outcome could belong to either – the events are not mutually exclusive, and you must watch for double counting.

concepts.title: Experimental Probability and the Law of Large Numbers
concepts.explanation:
Theoretical probability tells you what should happen if everything is fair and perfectly balanced. But real coins are slightly worn, real dice have tiny flaws, and some situations have no neat theory at all. In those cases we run an experiment and use the results. Experimental probability, also called relative frequency, is defined as:

Experimental probability = number of times the event happened ÷ total number of trials.

Suppose Hassan flips a coin 100 times and gets 47 heads. His experimental probability of heads is 47/100 = 0.47. The theoretical value is 0.5, so his result is close but not exactly equal. That difference is completely normal – it is just the natural variation you get in any finite experiment. If he flipped only 10 times he might get 7 heads (0.7) or 3 heads (0.3), values that stray much further from 0.5. Small samples wander; that is their nature.

Here is the key idea, known as the Law of Large Numbers: as the number of trials grows, the experimental probability tends to settle down towards the theoretical probability. Flip a fair coin ten times and heads might land on 30% or 70% of them. Flip it a thousand times and the fraction of heads will almost always sit very close to 50%. More trials means a more reliable estimate. This is exactly why scientists repeat experiments many times rather than trusting a single result.
concepts.example: Experimental probability also lets you predict an expected frequency – how many times you expect an event over many trials. If P(green) on a spinner is 1/4 and Khadija spins 40 times, she expects about 40 × 1/4 = 10 greens. 'Expected' does not mean she will get exactly 10 – she might get 8 or 12 – but 10 is the best single prediction. Expected frequency = probability × number of trials.

concepts.title: Sample Space Diagrams and Two-Way Tables
concepts.explanation:
When an experiment has two stages – rolling two dice, flipping two coins, or spinning then rolling – the neatest way to see every possible result is a sample space diagram. This is a grid that lists all the combinations. Because you can see every outcome, you can count the favourable ones directly and read off the probability.

Take rolling two dice and looking at the total. One die gives 6 outcomes; a second die also gives 6; together there are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. If you make a 6-by-6 grid with the first die down the side and the second die across the top, each cell holds one total. Counting the cells shows, for example, that a total of 7 appears in 6 cells, so P(total = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6. A total of 2 appears in just 1 cell (1 and 1), so P(2) = 1/36. A total of 11 appears in 2 cells (5 and 6, 6 and 5), so P(11) = 2/36 = 1/18.

A two-way table organises data by two categories at once, and it is perfect for probability drawn from real surveys. Imagine a survey of 75 students recording favourite subject against whether they are boys or girls. The rows are Boys and Girls, the columns are Maths, Science and English, and the final row and column hold the totals.
concepts.example: You read probabilities straight from the table. P(likes Maths) = 25/75 = 1/3, because 25 of the 75 students chose Maths. P(is a girl) = 40/75 = 8/15. P(is a girl and likes Science) = 18/75 = 6/25, using the single cell where the Girls row meets the Science column. You can even find a conditional probability – the chance of one thing given another. P(likes Science given the student is a girl) = 18/40 = 9/20, because you now look only at the 40 girls and ask how many of them chose Science. Two-way tables make these calculations tidy and reliable.

concepts.title: Independent Events and the Multiplication Rule
concepts.explanation:
Two events are independent when the outcome of one has no effect on the outcome of the other. Flipping a coin and rolling a die are independent: the coin does not know or care what the die does. For independent events there is a clean rule for the chance that both happen:

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) (for independent events).

So the probability of flipping a head and rolling a 6 is P(head) × P(6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. The probability that two rolled dice both show 6 is 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36 – which agrees with the sample space diagram in Concept 5, where '6 and 6' was 1 cell out of 36. Multiplying works because each of the 6 outcomes of the first die pairs with each of the 6 outcomes of the second.

Watch the language carefully. 'And' with independent events means multiply; 'or' with mutually exclusive events means add. Mixing these up is one of the most common errors in the whole topic, so pause each time and ask: am I combining outcomes into a single bigger set (or, add), or am I asking for two things to happen together (and, multiply)?
concepts.example: A famous trap here is the gambler's fallacy. After tossing five heads in a row, it feels as though tails is 'due'. It is not. Each toss is independent, so the probability of the next head is still 1/2, no matter what came before. Coins have no memory. The five past heads do not change the future; a run of heads is unusual, but from any point onward each new toss is a fresh 50-50 event.

methods.title: How to find a simple probability
methods.example: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green beads. One bead is drawn at random. Find P(blue).
steps: Count the total number of equally likely outcomes.
Count the favourable outcomes (the ones you want).
Divide favourable by total.
Simplify, and convert to a decimal or percentage if asked.

methods.title: Decide: is it 'and' (both) or 'or' (either)?
methods.example: A fair die is rolled. Find P(rolling a 2 or a 5).
steps: For 'or' with mutually exclusive events, add the probabilities.
For 'and' with independent events, multiply the probabilities.
Check whether replacement affects the second probability.

methods.title: How to use a tree diagram
methods.example: A fair coin is flipped twice. Draw a tree diagram to find P(exactly one head).
steps: Draw branches for the first event with probabilities.
From each outcome, draw branches for the second event.
Multiply along each path to get its probability.
Add the paths that give the outcome you want.

methods.title: Experimental probability and expected frequency
methods.example: Farah rolls a die 60 times and gets these results — 1: 8, 2: 12, 3: 9, 4: 11, 5: 10, 6: 10. Find the experimental probability of an even number, and compare it with the theoretical value. How many evens would she expect in 300 rolls?
steps: Evens are 2, 4 and 6, giving 12 + 11 + 10 = 33 even results out of 60.
Experimental P(even) = 33/60 = 11/20 = 0.55.
Theoretical P(even) = 3/6 = 0.5.
They are close; the small difference is normal variation.

methods.title: Sample space for two dice
methods.example: Two fair dice are rolled and the totals added. Find P(total = 8) and P(total is greater than 9).
steps: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes.
A total of 8 comes from (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) — that is 5 outcomes — so P(8) = 5/36.
A total greater than 9 means 10, 11 or 12: totals of 10 give 3 outcomes, 11 gives 2, and 12 gives 1, so 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 outcomes, giving P(> 9) = 6/36 = 1/6.

methods.title: Independent events (multiply)
methods.example: A coin is flipped and a die is rolled. Find P(head and a number greater than 4).
steps: These are independent.
P(head) = 1/2.
'Greater than 4' means 5 or 6, so P(> 4) = 2/6 = 1/3.
Therefore P(head and > 4) = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

workedExamples.title: Basic theoretical probability
workedExamples.prompt: A bag contains 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green beads. One bead is drawn at random. Find P(blue).
workedExamples.solution: Total beads = 5 + 3 + 2 = 10. Favourable (blue) = 3. So P(blue) = 3/10 = 0.3 = 30%. Always add up the whole collection first to get the total, then count the favourable outcomes.

workedExamples.title: Using the complement
workedExamples.prompt: Using the same bag (5 red, 3 blue, 2 green), find P(not green).
workedExamples.solution: P(green) = 2/10 = 1/5. So P(not green) = 1 − 1/5 = 4/5 = 0.8. Check the long way: P(red) + P(blue) = 5/10 + 3/10 = 8/10 = 4/5. The complement was faster and gave the same answer.

workedExamples.title: Mutually exclusive 'or'
workedExamples.prompt: A fair die is rolled. Find P(rolling a 1 or a 6).
workedExamples.solution: 'Rolling a 1' and 'rolling a 6' cannot both happen on one roll, so they are mutually exclusive. P(1 or 6) = P(1) + P(6) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3.

workedExamples.title: Experimental probability and expected frequency
workedExamples.prompt: Farah rolls a die 60 times and gets these results — 1: 8, 2: 12, 3: 9, 4: 11, 5: 10, 6: 10. Find the experimental probability of an even number, and compare it with the theoretical value. How many evens would she expect in 300 rolls?
workedExamples.solution: Evens are 2, 4 and 6, giving 12 + 11 + 10 = 33 even results out of 60. Experimental P(even) = 33/60 = 11/20 = 0.55. Theoretical P(even) = 3/6 = 0.5. They are close; the small difference is normal variation. Expected evens in 300 rolls = 0.5 × 300 = 150.

workedExamples.title: Sample space for two dice
workedExamples.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled and the totals added. Find P(total = 8) and P(total is greater than 9).
workedExamples.solution: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. A total of 8 comes from (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) — that is 5 outcomes — so P(8) = 5/36. A total greater than 9 means 10, 11 or 12: totals of 10 give 3 outcomes, 11 gives 2, and 12 gives 1, so 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 outcomes, giving P(> 9) = 6/36 = 1/6.

workedExamples.title: Independent events (multiply)
workedExamples.prompt: A coin is flipped and a die is rolled. Find P(head and a number greater than 4).
workedExamples.solution: These are independent. P(head) = 1/2. 'Greater than 4' means 5 or 6, so P(> 4) = 2/6 = 1/3. Therefore P(head and > 4) = 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6.

workedExamples.title: Tree diagram, two flips
workedExamples.prompt: A fair coin is flipped twice. Find P(exactly one head).
workedExamples.solution: The four equally likely paths are HH, HT, TH, TT, each 1/4. 'Exactly one head' means HT or TH, so P = 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2. Note that 'exactly one head' is different from 'at least one head' (which would also include HH).

workedExamples.title: Dependent events, without replacement
workedExamples.prompt: A bag has 4 red and 2 blue beads. Two beads are drawn without replacement. Find P(both red) and P(one of each colour).
workedExamples.solution: First draw P(red) = 4/6. After removing one red, 3 red and 2 blue remain, so second draw P(red) = 3/5. P(both red) = 4/6 × 3/5 = 12/30 = 2/5. For one of each: P(red then blue) = 4/6 × 2/5 = 8/30, and P(blue then red) = 2/6 × 4/5 = 8/30. Add the two paths: 8/30 + 8/30 = 16/30 = 8/15.

workedExamples.title: A spinner lands on green with probability 2/5. In 80…
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner lands on green with probability 2/5. In 80 spins, how many greens are expected?
workedExamples.solution: P(green) = 2/5. Expected number of greens in 80 spins = 2/5 × 80 = 32.

workedExamples.title: A coin is flipped and a die rolled. Find P(head and a…
workedExamples.prompt: A coin is flipped and a die rolled. Find P(head and a 3) and P(tail and an even number).
workedExamples.solution: These are independent events. P(head) = 1/2 and P(3) = 1/6, so P(head and a 3) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12. P(tail) = 1/2 and P(even number) = 3/6 = 1/2, so P(tail and an even number) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

workedExamples.title: Two fair dice are rolled. Using a sample space…
workedExamples.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Using a sample space diagram, find P(total = 6) and P(total = 9).
workedExamples.solution: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. A total of 6 comes from (1,5), (2,4), (3,3), (4,2), (5,1) — 5 outcomes — so P(total = 6) = 5/36. A total of 9 comes from (3,6), (4,5), (5,4), (6,3) — 4 outcomes — so P(total = 9) = 4/36 = 1/9.

activities.title: The Great Coin Experiment
steps: Flip the coin 10 times and record how many heads you get. Work out the experimental P(heads).
Now flip it another 40 times (50 in total) and update your experimental P(heads).
Keep going to 100 flips if you can, updating the fraction each time.
Watch how the fraction moves. Does it drift towards 0.5 as the number of flips grows? Write a sentence explaining what the Law of Large Numbers predicts.
Keep your results table – it is proof of the Law of Large Numbers in action.

activities.title: Two-Dice Totals Investigation
activities.materials: two dice, paper for a tally chart.
steps: Before rolling, predict which total (from 2 to 12) will come up most often, and which least often.
Roll the two dice 50 times, adding the numbers each time, and tally each total.
Draw a bar chart of your totals. Which total won? Which was rarest?
Now build the 6-by-6 sample space of all 36 outcomes and count how many give each total. Compare the theory with your experiment.
You should find 7 is the most likely total (6 ways out of 36) and 2 and 12 the least likely (1 way each). Did your experiment agree?

activities.title: Design a Fair Game
activities.materials: dice, a coin, or a home-made spinner; paper.
steps: Invent a simple two-player game of chance – for example, Player A wins if two coins match, Player B wins if they differ.
Work out each player's theoretical probability of winning.
Decide whether your game is fair (equal chances). If it is not, change a rule to make it fair.
Test the game 20 times with a partner, or by playing both roles yourself if no partner is available, and compare the actual win rates with your theory.
For the two-coin example, both HH/TT (match) and HT/TH (differ) give 2 out of 4, so that game is already fair – can you design one that is not, then fix it?

activities.title: Beads Without Replacement
activities.materials: a small bag or cup and 8 beads or beans in two colours (say 5 dark, 3 light).
steps: Without looking, draw one bead, record its colour, and do not put it back.
Draw a second bead and record whether you got two of the same colour or one of each.
Return the beads and repeat the whole two-draw trial 20 times, tallying the results.
Compare your experimental results with the theory: P(both dark) = 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 = 5/14. How close were you?
This shows dependent events in action – the first draw really does change the chances for the second.

activities.title: Family Two-Way Table Survey
activities.materials: family members or classmates to survey, paper for a table.
steps: Choose two yes/no or category questions – for example, 'Do you prefer bariis or anjero?' and 'Male or female?'.
Survey at least 15 people and record each answer.
Organise your results in a two-way table with row and column totals.
Calculate five different probabilities from your table, including at least one conditional probability such as P(prefers bariis given male).
Present your table to your teacher (or your AI tutor if your teacher is not available) and explain one interesting relationship you found in the data.

activities.title: Weather Forecast Detective
activities.materials: access to a daily weather forecast for your city, a notebook.
steps: For one week, write down the forecast chance of rain each day (for example, '30% chance').
Each evening, record whether it actually rained.
At the end of the week, compare the forecasts with reality. On the days the forecast said 70% or more, did it usually rain?
Write a short paragraph on what '30% chance of rain' really means and why weather is described with probability.

After your activities, talk or write about these questions: How did your experimental results compare with the theoretical predictions? What happened to the accuracy as you did more trials? Which activity made the difference between independent and dependent events clearest? Which idea would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher, or with your AI tutor if you want feedback sooner.

rules.title: The 0-to-1 Rule
rules.text: Because every probability lies between 0 and 1, you have a built-in check on your own work. If you ever calculate a probability that is negative, or greater than 1, you have made a mistake somewhere – stop and find it. A probability of 2, or of −0.3, simply cannot exist. This single rule, 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, will catch many errors before they cost you marks.

rules.title: The Sum-to-1 Rule
rules.text: This 'sum to 1' rule is another powerful check. If Yusuf calculates the chances of the four spinner colours and they add up to more than 1, he knows at once that he has slipped somewhere. Keep it in your toolkit alongside the 0-to-1 rule from Concept 1.

rules.title: The Complement Rule
rules.text: The complement of an event A is simply 'A does not happen'. Because an event either happens or it does not, these two possibilities must together cover everything, so their probabilities add to 1. That gives a very useful rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

rules.title: The Independent Multiplication Rule
rules.text: Two events are independent when the outcome of one has no effect on the outcome of the other. Flipping a coin and rolling a die are independent: the coin does not know or care what the die does. For independent events there is a clean rule for the chance that both happen: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

rules.title: Unit Summary: Seven Big Ideas
rules.text: You have now met seven big ideas: the probability scale, theoretical probability, complements and mutually exclusive events, experimental probability with the Law of Large Numbers, sample space diagrams and two-way tables, independent events with the multiplication rule, and tree diagrams with dependent events. These ideas are not separate islands – they work as one toolkit.

commonMistakes: Thinking a coin or die is "due" a result — each trial is independent of past results.
Forgetting that removing an item without replacement changes the probabilities for the next draw.
Assuming P(A|B) = P(B|A) — these are usually different.

A fair coin is flipped three times. Draw a tree diagram and find P(exactly two heads) and P(at least one head).
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Eight equally likely paths, each 1/8; exactly two heads = HHT, HTH, THH → 3/8; at least one head = 1 − P(TTT) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. Find P(total is a multiple of 4). (Multiples of 4 are 4, 8 and 12.)
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Total 4 → 3 outcomes, total 8 → 5, total 12 → 1, so 3 + 5 + 1 = 9, giving 9/36 = 1/4.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A test has probability 0.8 of a student passing. Two students sit it independently. Find P(both pass), P(both fail) and P(exactly one passes).
Explain the key idea in Sample Space Diagrams and Two-Way Tables.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: When an experiment has two stages – rolling two dice, flipping two coins, or spinning then rolling – the neatest way to see every possible result is a sample space diagram. This is a grid that lists all the combinations. Because you can see every outcome, you can count the favourable ones directly and read off the probability. Take rolling two dice and looking at the total. One die gives 6 outcomes; a second die also gives 6; together there are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. If you make a 6-by-6 grid with the totals filled in, you can count how many cells give any target total and read its probability straight off the diagram.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Independent Events and the Multiplication Rule.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Two events are independent when the outcome of one has no effect on the outcome of the other. Flipping a coin and rolling a die are independent: the coin does not know or care what the die does. For independent events there is a clean rule for the chance that both happen: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) (for independent events).

The set of all possible outcomes
An outcome or group of outcomes you want
The event 'not A'; P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
rounds.answer: A single possible result of a trial
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 13 Maths Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Outcome means a single possible result of a trial.

rounds.prompt: On the probability scale, which value means an event is certain to happen?
rounds.clue: Think about what each end of the 0-to-1 scale represents.
rounds.explanation: A probability of 1 means the event is certain; 0 means impossible, and 0.5 means an even chance.

rounds.prompt: If P(it rains tomorrow) = 0.3, what is P(it does not rain tomorrow)?
rounds.clue: Use the complement rule: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

rounds.prompt: A spinner lands on red with probability 1/4. If it is spun 120 times, how many reds are expected?
rounds.clue: Expected frequency = probability × number of trials.

games.title: Mastery Mix: Sample space
games.description: Four short challenges on Sample space.

rounds.prompt: What does “Sample space” mean?
choices: The set of all possible outcomes
An outcome or group of outcomes you want
The event 'not A'; P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
Events that cannot both happen at once
rounds.answer: The set of all possible outcomes
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 13 Maths Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Sample space means the set of all possible outcomes.

rounds.prompt: A bag contains 3 red counters and 7 blue counters. One counter is drawn at random. What is P(red)?
rounds.clue: P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes.
rounds.explanation: There are 3 red counters out of 10 total, so P(red) = 3/10.

rounds.prompt: A fair die is rolled. What is P(rolling a 2 or a 5)?
rounds.clue: For mutually exclusive events, add the individual probabilities.

rounds.prompt: Two fair coins are flipped together. Using a sample space diagram, how many equally likely outcomes are there?
rounds.clue: List every combination: HH, HT, TH, TT.
rounds.explanation: Each coin has 2 outcomes, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 equally likely outcomes in the sample space.

rounds.prompt: What does “Event” mean?
choices: An outcome or group of outcomes you want
The event 'not A'; P(not A) = 1 − P(A)
Events that cannot both happen at once
One outcome does not affect the other
rounds.answer: An outcome or group of outcomes you want
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 13 Maths Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Event means an outcome or group of outcomes you want.

rounds.prompt: Write the probability 3/4 as a percentage.
rounds.clue: Divide the numerator by the denominator, then multiply by 100.

rounds.prompt: A coin is flipped 50 times and lands on heads 21 times. What is the experimental probability of heads?
rounds.clue: Experimental probability = number of successes ÷ number of trials.
rounds.explanation: 21 heads out of 50 flips gives an experimental probability of 21/50 = 0.42.

rounds.prompt: Which of these events has a probability closest to 0?
choices: Rolling an even number on a fair die
The sun rising tomorrow
Picking a red ball from a bag of 1 red and 99 blue balls
Flipping a coin and getting heads or tails
rounds.answer: Picking a red ball from a bag of 1 red and 99 blue balls
rounds.clue: The event closest to 0 is the least likely to happen.
rounds.explanation: P(red) = 1/100 = 0.01, which is very close to 0 (impossible), making it the least likely event listed.

selfAssessment: I can describe probability as a measure of likelihood on a scale from 0 to 1.
I can calculate theoretical probability for equally likely outcomes using the basic formula.
I can express a probability as a fraction, decimal or percentage and convert between them.
I can find the probability of an event not happening using the complement.
I can add probabilities for mutually exclusive events.
I can run experiments to find experimental probability (relative frequency) and compare it with theory.
I can use the idea of expected frequency to predict results over many trials.
I can list all outcomes with a sample space diagram or two-way table.
